e.etymology: An African American name that peaked around 1990, built on the -esha sound of Aisha and Iesha with a T- opening.
A phonetic spelling of Danielle, the French feminine of Daniel, from Hebrew Daniyyel, 'God is my judge'.
A common misspelling of Keith, a Scottish surname from the lands of Keith in East Lothian. The place name is probably from a Brittonic word for 'wood', related to Welsh coed.
A respelling of Daryl or Darrell, an English surname from Norman d'Airelle, 'from Airelle', a village in Normandy.
From an old Germanic name joining hild, 'battle', and red, 'counsel'. It came back into use in the late 1800s alongside Mildred and was given to both girls and boys.
A respelling of Brittany, the English name of the region of northwest France settled by Britons in the 5th century. Brittany became a popular American girls' name in the 1980s.
A spelling of Pearl, the English word for the gem, from Old French perle. Pearl became a given name in the 1800s, when jewel names came into fashion.

assoc.t: Pearle Vision, the eye care and eyeglasses chain

e.etymology: An American name of the 1960s that crosses Tammy with the ending of Samantha and Tabitha, the mother and daughter of the TV series Bewitched.
A French feminine form of George, from Greek georgos, 'farmer', literally 'earth worker'.
An elaboration of Ruth with a feminine -a, used in the American South in the early 1900s. Ruth, the loyal daughter-in-law of the Bible, probably comes from Hebrew re'ut, 'friend'.
A feminine elaboration of Bernard with the -etta ending, used in the US in the early 1900s. Bernard comes from Germanic bern, 'bear', and hard, 'brave, strong'.
A pet form of Tennessee, which was given to girls in the 19th-century South. The stockbroker and suffragist Tennessee Claflin went by Tennie.
A spelling of Tamika, an American name of the 1960s and 70s thought to come from Japanese Tamiko, which reached US audiences through the 1962 film A Girl Named Tamiko.
A spelling of Glenys, a Welsh name coined in the late 1800s, probably from glân, 'pure, clean, holy'. Chuck Yeager named the plane that broke the sound barrier Glamorous Glennis after his wife.
A surname used as a first name in the American South, where the Baptist leader Richard Furman, for whom Furman University is named, was widely honored.
A spelling of Lonnie, a pet form of Alonzo for boys and of Leona and Apollonia for girls. Alonzo is a form of Alfonso, from Germanic words for 'noble' and 'ready'.
An American name of the 1960s that adds the Spanish-style ending -ita to the sound of Denise, or makes a feminine of Dennis. Both go back to Greek Dionysios, 'of Dionysus'.
A spelling of Jennie or Genie, used as a pet form of Geneva, Genevieve, Eugenia and Virginia.
A respelling of Megan, a Welsh pet form of Meg, short for Margaret, from Greek margarites, 'pearl'. The a spelling reflects the MAY-gun pronunciation.
The standard written abbreviation of William, entered as a name in its own right in old US records. William comes from Germanic wil, 'will', and helm, 'helmet, protection'.
e.note: An abbreviation, not a separate name; it is read aloud as William.

e.etymology: A respelling of Regina, Latin for 'queen'. Christians used it in honor of the Virgin Mary as Regina Caeli, Queen of Heaven.
A respelling of Sandy, the pet form of Sandra and Alexandra, from Greek alexein, 'to defend', and aner, 'man'.
A variant of Durward, a Scottish and English surname from the Middle English for doorkeeper, reshaped with the familiar -wood ending.
An American coinage of the 1970s and 1980s that joins the Shan- opening with the -eka ending of Tameka.
A surname used as a first name, a spelling of Leaman or Lemon, which goes back to the Middle English leofman, beloved man or sweetheart.
A spelling of Christine, the French form of Christina, from Latin Christiana, a follower of Christ.
A spelling of Eloise, from the Old French Heloise, which probably goes back to the Germanic name Helewidis, built from words for healthy and wide.
A spelling of Lawrence, from the Roman name Laurentius, a man from Laurentum, an ancient town near Rome whose name was linked with the laurel tree.
An American name of the 1970s and 1980s built on the Shar- of Sharon with the Spanish-style -ita ending.
An English surname used as a first name, mostly in the American South.
